<p class="session-lead">What changes when we scale the model—and how should we spend the compute?</p>

<p class="route-question">Is a larger model the best use of a fixed training-compute budget?</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 1 minute, included in the first 10-minute section. Revised with the instructor
on 12 November: sentiment is the sole worked application. Detailed NER/QA and the
small BERT-tiny experiment are removed from the active deck but retained as optional
source material. The NER-based frozen-feature comparison is also optional.

The remaining agenda is a proposal, not authored slides. Follow the supplied
Stanford PDF viewer pages 42–56 (printed slides 44 onward): GPT transfer, GPT-2,
GPT-3 and in-context learning, scaling laws, compute allocation, and what models
learn or memorize. Use primary-paper figures, with readable axes and stated settings.
Correct historical source metadata rather than copying slide typos (GPT-2 is 2019).

Distinguish Kaplan et al. (2020) from Hoffmann et al. (2022): empirical scaling
studies lead to different allocation recommendations. Chinchilla compares fewer
parameters and more tokens under approximately the same training-compute budget
as Gopher; this is not a claim that it used more total training compute. Training
and inference efficiency are distinct, and a compute-optimal rule is not universal.

Final item: 10 minutes on capabilities, memorization, bias, and limitations, then
5 minutes bridging to instruction following. Instruction tuning, preference
optimization, LoRA, adapters, and quantization remain in Lecture 09.
:::
